newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, U.S. to discuss grain subsidies, biotech.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. to discuss grain subsidies, biotech.

text.p: Senior European Commission and U.S. agriculture officials were due to meet on Tuesday evening to discuss EU policy on wheat export subsidies, imports of gene-altered soybeans and maize, Commission sources said.

Guy Legras, Commission Director General for Agriculture, was expected to reassure Paul Drazek, senior trade adviser to U.S. Agriculture Secretary, Dan Glickman, that the EU did not intend to undercut U.S. wheat prices.
Drazek was also due to meet officials in the Commission's international farm trade division.
Both sides were saying little before the meetings in a bid to play down expectations and prevent trade tensions mounting.
"It's only a technical discussion," said a Commission source, noting that EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler would not be involved.

The source added that Drazek was stopping off on his way to Geneva to observe a World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute panel hearing on Thursday of a U.S. complaint against an EU ban on imports of meat treated with growth hormones.
The U.S. has criticised the EU's resumption last month of wheat export susbidies after a year-long pause and warned that it would fight subsidies with subsidies if necessary.

Following a massive EU harvest and bigger crops in many major grain-producing countries, Washington is concerned that wheat prices will continue to slide and prompt increasing use of export subsidies.
Wheat prices have nearly halved since peaking at $300 a tonne earlier this year.
On biotechnology, Drazek is expected to press the EU to speed up approval of genetically-modified maize produced by Swiss company Ciba-Geigy AG before the U.S. crop is harvested.
The maize has been altered to resist the corn borer pest.

The EU earlier this year approved the use of genetically-altered "Roundup Ready" soybeans developed by Monsanto despite protests by environmentalists. The beans are resistant to the company's Roundup herbicide.

Some European groups have called for transgenic soybeans and maize to be handled separately and clearly labelled, but the U.S. says that this is impractical and unnecessary because the products are safe.
